newsitem.title: BULGARIA: LEV CRISIS GIVES BULGARIA WORLD'S CHEAPEST BIG MAC.
newsitem.headline: LEV CRISIS GIVES BULGARIA WORLD'S CHEAPEST BIG MAC.

text.p: The collapse of the lev has allowed McDonald's Bulgaria to overtake China in offering the world's least expensive Big Mac hamburger in dollar terms.

But while the rapidly rising cost of imports has dismayed other foreign companies in a country whose industry depends on foreign inputs, McDonald's says it has operated through worse crises in other countries and is taking a long-term view.
The lev has fallen from 70 to the dollar at the beginning of the year to about 350 now, touching lows of 395 last week and hugely increasing the cost of imports.
McDonald's efforts to keep its hamburgers within the means of Bulgarian clients mean a Big Mac which cost the equivalent of $1.50 at the beginning of the year, now costs $1.10.
"We adapt ourselves to the local economy," Managing Director Branislav Knezevic told Reuters.
He said McDonald's Bulgaria had increased the proportion of domestically-produced inputs and was using local suppliers to build and furnish new restaurants.
"The devaluation made us much faster in finding local suppliers," Knezevic said, that the company was now exporting Bulgarian-made signs and tabletops to other McDonalds operations in the region.
Knezevic said McDonald's financial planners had seen the Bulgarian economy heading for meltdown two years ago as cumulative devaluation failed to match inflation.
"We're taking a long-term view," he said. "This crisis had a beginning and will also have an end."
He said McDonald's was committed to the Bulgarian market but other foreign investors complain Bulgaria has the least favourable business climate in the region.
Interest rates are currently 180 percent, and excessive red tape and inconsistent legislation also deter investment in a relatively small market of 8.4 million people.
Knezevic, a Yugoslav, said all markets presented their own difficulties and the McDonald's Corp presence was an important signal to other investors.
"If McDonald's is in a market, it is a flagship for other foreign investors in the future," he said.

Like other foreign businessmen, he welcomed the government's plans to introduce a currency board, which will force the central bank to match levs in circulation with foreign exchange reserves, effectively pegging the lev probably to the dollar and stopping the bank printing money.
"Things will be tough for the first three months then after that quite good," he said.
The company imports some 85 percent of ingredients, including meat, french fries and condiments, but the 15 percent that are locally produced account for 40 percent of sales.
"The big cost of imports is offset by Bulgarian suppliers," Knezevic said. Local products include buns, dairy products, salads, and some of the boxes and wrappings.

Knezevic said McDonald's had revised its prices on average twice a month since the start of the year to take account of inflation, which reached a cumulative 195 percent for the first 10 months of 1996 before last week's run on dollars sent the lev falling further.
McDonald's opened its first restaurant in Bulgaria in 1994 and now has five outlets, with another three under construction. It hopes to open one more restaurant this year and four in 1997.
